implementation_notes: With lapin the dead-letter channel is declared through the queue's FieldTable: insert x-dead-letter-exchange (and optionally x-dead-letter-routing-key) as AMQP field values while declaring the source queue, then call Channel::basic_reject(delivery_tag, requeue=false) or basic_nack when the handler decides the message is dead; the broker routes it to the DLX on reject, TTL expiry or queue-length overflow. The DLQ consumer reads the x-death header from the delivery properties to recover the original queue and reason. When the application itself republishes dead letters instead of relying on the broker, enable the publisher-confirm extension and await the confirmation, otherwise the hop is best-effort and can lose the record it was meant to preserve.
pitfalls: lapin is async and channel operations are ordered: awaiting a reject inside a consumer while another task publishes on the same channel can deadlock - use separate channels or a cloned connection.
FieldTable values are typed AMQP values, so a Rust &str where LongString is expected fails at declare/publish time, not at compile time.
Delivery tags are per-channel and reset after recovery: rejecting a tag from before a reconnect closes the channel instead of dead-lettering the message.
A DLQ with no consumer fails nothing in Rust and produces no error - it simply grows, so monitoring must live outside the type system.

variants.name: rdkafka consumer publishing to a <topic>.DLT topic
variants.idiom_name: rdkafka StreamConsumer + BaseProducer with error headers, commit after delivery
variants.implementation_notes: Kafka has no broker-side dead-lettering, so the Rust realization is explicit: on a permanent processing failure build a dead-letter record - original payload plus headers with source topic, partition, offset, error and attempt count - produce it to <topic>.DLT with rdkafka's BaseProducer, wait for the delivery report, and only then commit the source offset. Committing inside the catch without waiting for that report is what turns the dead-letter hop into a lossy step, because send() only enqueues into the producer's buffer. Keeping the original key on the DLT record preserves per-key ordering inside the dead-letter topic, which matters when a whole key's stream has to be replayed together.
pitfalls: Committing before the delivery report arrives makes the dead-letter hop lossy; send() returns as soon as the record is in the producer's queue.
The DLT topic must exist with enough retention (or auto-creation must be enabled): when the producer's queue fills, records are dropped and only logged.
Kafka consumption is at-least-once, so a rebalance can redeliver the original after its DLT copy exists - deduplicate DLT records by original topic/partition/offset when replaying.
The DLT producer needs its own error callback and queue bounds; sharing configuration with the main producer couples dead-letter capacity to business throughput.
